summaries.gardner: Arista fits most Rule Breaker traits: it is a top dog in AI and cloud data-centre networking, the shares are up about 37% in a year and about 700% in five years, it is led by long-time CEO Jayshree Ullal with co-founders Andy Bechtolsheim and Ken Duda, and it is widely called expensive at about 62 times trailing earnings. Its weaker points for Gardner are a low consumer profile and reliance on Microsoft and Meta for 42% of revenue.
summaries.buffett: Arista has many Buffett traits: no debt, $13.3B of cash and investments, a 39% net margin, a return on equity near 28% and consistent growth since its 2014 IPO. But its technology changes fast, two customers dominate sales, and at about 62 times trailing earnings and 47 times forward earnings there is no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire Arista's engineering culture, rational capital use and lean cost base, which deliver a 42.8% operating margin without debt. Inverting, the main ways it could fail are a capex pause by Microsoft or Meta, NVIDIA bundling networking with GPUs, or white-box switches, and the price leaves little room for those risks.
summaries.lynch: Arista is a clear fast grower (revenue up 28.6% in 2025 and guided up about 40% in 2026) with a simple story: more AI and cloud data centres need more high-speed switches. Lynch would object to the price, as a trailing P/E near 62 is well above its earnings growth of roughly 25-40%, and it is a widely owned Wall Street favourite rather than an overlooked stock.
summaries.fisher: Arista scores well on Fisher's points: it keeps launching new platforms (800G, 1.6T, campus, VeloCloud SD-WAN), spends $1,237M a year on R&D that turns into share gains, has very high margins and has a long-serving, candid management team. The main gaps are heavy customer concentration and insider selling.
summaries.graham: Arista fails Graham's defensive tests on price and dividends: it pays no dividend, trades at about 62 times trailing earnings and 16.9 times book value, and P/E times P/B is far above 22.5. It does pass on size, financial strength (no debt, current ratio near 3) and an unbroken profit record.
summaries.thiel: Arista answers many of Thiel's questions well: it started by dominating a small niche (low-latency switches for trading firms and early cloud builders), has a strong team and a direct sales channel to hyperscalers, and is riding the AI build-out at the right time. But its technology is better rather than ten times better than rivals, and its market is contested by NVIDIA, Cisco and white-box makers.
summaries.gerstner: Arista fits Gerstner's focus on durable AI-infrastructure winners with real profits: revenue is growing about 36% in 2026 with a 43% operating margin and nearly 49% trailing free-cash-flow margin. The valuation, at about 47 times forward earnings, already assumes much of that growth, so price discipline is the main question.
summaries.druckenmiller: Arista has the earnings momentum Druckenmiller seeks: guidance was raised three times in 2026 to about $12.6B, it beat EPS estimates in each of the last eight quarters, and purchase commitments rose to $9.7B. The risk is that AI capex sentiment turns, which would hit a richly valued stock quickly.
summaries.smith: Arista meets Terry Smith's 'good company' tests: high returns on capital, a 64% gross margin, strong cash conversion (2025 free cash flow of $4,252M vs net income of $3,511M) and no debt. Whether it is 'not overpaying' is doubtful at a free-cash-flow yield of about 2%.
summaries.greenblatt: Arista's return on capital is very high, but its earnings yield is low: operating income of about $4.5B over the last twelve months is only about 1.9% of an enterprise value near $236B. It would therefore rank well on quality but poorly on price in the Magic Formula.
summaries.akre: Arista has two legs of Akre's stool: a wonderful business with high returns, and capable, honest-seeming management led by Jayshree Ullal since 2008. The third leg, reinvestment, is weaker: it generates far more cash than it can reinvest, building a $13.3B cash pile and buying back shares rather than compounding retained earnings at high rates.
summaries.pabrai: Arista is a low-debt, simple-to-explain business, but it is not a Dhandho bet: there is no distress, no temporary setback and no low price, so the 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' asymmetry is missing at about 62 times trailing earnings.
summaries.wood: Arista is a direct beneficiary of AI, one of ARK's main innovation platforms, through its Etherlink AI networking (at least $3.5B targeted in 2026). It is an established, profitable hardware vendor rather than a pure disruptive platform, and its costs fall with Broadcom's chip roadmap rather than through Wright's-law-style learning of its own.
summaries.ackman: Arista fits several of Ackman's criteria: a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative business with high barriers, no debt and strong management. It lacks the discount to intrinsic value he wants, and its revenue depends heavily on the capex cycles of a few cloud giants.
summaries.sleep: Arista partly fits Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared ideal: it passes the cost benefits of merchant silicon and software to large customers, keeping prices competitive, and has a long-term owner-like culture. But its advantage depends on technology cycles and two big customers more than on a self-reinforcing flywheel.
summaries.valentine: Arista fits Don Valentine's test of a huge, fast-growing market with a hard technical problem: moving AI and cloud traffic at 800G-1.6T speeds. It was founded by engineers (Bechtolsheim, Cheriton, Duda) to solve that problem and has become the clear independent leader.
summaries.nash: Arista passes most of Tom Nash's checks: no debt, 28.6% revenue growth in 2025 with a 42.8% operating margin, eight straight EPS beats and a scorecard of 110 out of 130. It falls short on valuation: the 12% Nash DCF gives about $112 a share against a $195.42 price, the PEG is about 1.2, and its CEO sells rather than buys shares.

momentum.evidence: The shares rose about 37% in the year to October 14, 2026 ($143.02 to $195.42) and about 55% in six months, against roughly 16% for the S&P 500 (SPY) over the year.

g4.evidence: CEO Jayshree Ullal has led Arista since 2008 alongside co-founders Andy Bechtolsheim (Sun co-founder and first Google investor) and Ken Duda, and its largest partners include Microsoft, Meta and Broadcom.

g6.evidence: Commentators often call it expensive, for example Trefis's September 2026 piece 'Is Arista Networks Stock As Expensive As It Looks?' noted 58.3 times trailing adjusted earnings.

simple.evidence: The core idea (selling the switches that link servers and AI chips in data centres) is easy to grasp, but judging its technology edge against NVIDIA, Cisco and white boxes needs specialist knowledge.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $2,317.5M in 2020 to $9,005.7M in 2025 and net income from $634.6M to $3,511.4M.

integrity.evidence: Management gives clear, conservative guidance and has no debt or empire-building, but co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim settled SEC insider-trading charges in 2024 over trades in another company and left the board, and insiders sell regularly.

b6.evidence: Arista has made only small, focused acquisitions (such as Big Switch and Awake Security in 2020 and VeloCloud from Broadcom in 2025) and keeps a lean cost base, with sales and marketing at 5.9% of 2025 revenue.

roic.evidence: With no debt, 2025 net income of $3,511.4M was about 28% of year-end equity of $12,370.5M, much of which is cash, so the return on operating capital is far higher.

fcf.evidence: 2025 free cash flow was $4,252.4M ($4,371.9M operating cash flow less $119.5M capex), 121% of net income of $3,511.4M.

b10.evidence: Shareholders' equity grew from $4,885.8M at end-2022 to $14,797.7M in June 2026 while the market value rose to about $249B, far more than the profits retained.

safety.evidence: At $195.42 the stock trades at about 62 times trailing GAAP EPS of $3.16, and a Nash-style DCF at a 12% discount rate gives about $112 a share, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: About 47 times FY2026 consensus non-GAAP EPS of $4.12 is high, but revenue is guided up about 40% in 2026 with a 43% operating margin, so the premium is partly earned.

mu5.evidence: No debt and $13.3B of cash make financial failure unlikely, but 42% of 2025 revenue came from Microsoft and Meta, and NVIDIA's bundled networking or white boxes could erode its position.

reinvest.evidence: Arista reinvests heavily in R&D ($1,237.3M in 2025) at high returns, but it generates far more cash than it can use, so cash and investments grew to $13,343.3M.

ly2.evidence: Arista is a fast grower: revenue rose 28.6% in 2025 and 36.5% in the first half of 2026 on demand for AI and cloud data-centre switches.

ly3.evidence: The trailing GAAP P/E of about 62 is well above EPS growth of 23% in 2025 and 31% in the first half of 2026.

runway.evidence: Arista targets a $105B addressable market by 2029 and is expanding into campus, SD-WAN (VeloCloud) and scale-across AI networking, which it sizes at $15-20B by 2030.

ly7.evidence: Insiders sell rather than buy (a Form 144 for about $28.3M of stock was filed on October 9, 2026), and although Arista bought back $1,603.1M of stock in 2025, it bought none in the first half of 2026 and diluted shares are flat at about 1,276M.

ly8.evidence: Arista is an S&P 100 member covered by about 32 analysts, 31 of whom rate it a buy, so it is not overlooked.

fi2.evidence: Arista keeps refreshing its lines, moving from 400G to 800G and now 1.6T switches (the 7060X-E7 in 2026), and adding campus Wi-Fi, routing and VeloCloud SD-WAN as cloud switching matures.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $1,237.3M in 2025 (13.7% of revenue) has produced products that took Arista to 18.7% of data-centre Ethernet switching in 2Q26 and more than 100 Etherlink AI customers.

fi4.evidence: Arista wins with engineering-led selling and spent only 5.9% of 2025 revenue on sales and marketing, but its sales are concentrated in a few huge customers and its enterprise reach trails Cisco's.

longterm.evidence: Management invests ahead in new platforms such as 1.6T Ethernet, the Ultra Ethernet standard and campus, and accepts lower gross margins (62-64% guided for 2026) to win large AI deployments.

gr1.evidence: Arista is an S&P 100 company with about $249B of market value and $9,005.7M of 2025 revenue.

ni10.evidence: Arista has reported a net profit every year since its 2014 IPO, including $634.6M in 2020 and $3,511.4M in 2025.

gr4.evidence: Arista has never paid a dividend; it returns cash through share buybacks.

eps10.evidence: GAAP diluted EPS rose from about $0.50 in 2020 (split-adjusted $2.00) to $2.75 in 2025, more than five times in five years alone.

gr6.evidence: The price is about 62 times trailing GAAP EPS of $3.16 and far above 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 62 times a price-to-book of about 16.9 is roughly 1,040, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: EOS's single-image design and reliability are a clear edge, but Arista's switches use the same Broadcom chips as white-box rivals, so it is better rather than ten times better.

timing.evidence: The AI build-out is driving data-centre Ethernet switching up 64.5% year on year in 2Q26 (IDC), and Ethernet is displacing InfiniBand in AI back-end networks.

th3.evidence: Arista began with low-latency switches for high-frequency traders and early cloud builders and expanded to lead cloud data-centre switching and enter campus and routing.

team.evidence: Arista is led by Jayshree Ullal (CEO since 2008, ex-Cisco) with co-founders Andy Bechtolsheim and Ken Duda, a team with a long record in networking.

th5.evidence: It sells directly to cloud titans with joint engineering teams and through channel partners to over 10,000 enterprise and service-provider customers.

durable.evidence: EOS and its hyperscaler relationships have lasted 18 years, but networking technology shifts every few years and NVIDIA overtook it in data-centre Ethernet switching in 1Q26.

th7.evidence: Arista saw early that cloud networks needed merchant silicon and one programmable OS, a contrarian bet in 2008, but that idea is now widely copied.

trend.evidence: Arista is a leading beneficiary of AI and cloud computing, targeting at least $3.5B of AI fabrics revenue in 2026 and serving Microsoft and Meta's AI data centres.

dr1.evidence: 2026 revenue guidance was raised from $10.5B at Analyst Day to $11.5B in May and about $12.6B in August, and Arista beat consensus EPS in each of the last eight quarters.

dr2.evidence: Purchase commitments of $9.7B (vs $3.6B a year earlier), deferred revenue of $6.9B and 1.6T switches moving to production in 2027 point to further growth, though much of this is already expected.

dr4.evidence: With no debt Arista is not hurt by rates, and easy funding for AI data centres helps its customers spend, but a tighter economy or capital markets could slow cloud capex.

dr6.evidence: Q3 2026 results (guided to about $3.3B revenue), 1.6T production ramps in 2027 and new scale-across AI wins are identifiable catalysts.

dr7.evidence: The business quality and AI exposure support high conviction, but customer concentration and a rich valuation argue against a very large position.

gm.evidence: GAAP gross margin was 64.06% in 2025 and non-GAAP 63.4% in Q2 2026, high for hardware and a sign of pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $5,155M gives a yield of about 2.1% on a $249B market value, low in absolute terms but reasonable for 30%+ growth.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $4,547M is only about 1.9% of an enterprise value of roughly $236B.

pa2.evidence: Arista is not in a setback: revenue grew 36.5% in the first half of 2026 and guidance has been raised three times this year.

pa4.evidence: No debt and $13.3B of cash make permanent business loss unlikely, but the shares fell from about $133 to $59 between January and April 2025, showing how much a high multiple can fall.

wo1.evidence: Arista is a leader in AI networking, with AI fabrics revenue targeted at more than $3.5B in 2026 and more than 100 Etherlink AI customers.

wo2.evidence: Cost per bit falls quickly with each new Broadcom chip generation, driving huge demand, but memory and silicon costs rose in 2026 and pressured gross margin.

wo3.evidence: It combines AI networking with cloud computing and software (EOS, CloudVision, AVA AI operations), but not several of ARK's distinct platforms.

wo4.evidence: Arista sees its addressable market reaching $105B by 2029 and scale-across networking growing to $15-20B by 2030, large but not many times larger than today in five years.

ac3.evidence: With no debt it is insulated from interest rates, but memory and chip prices squeeze its gross margin and its sales track cloud giants' capex cycles.

ns1.evidence: Arista gives cloud titans lower prices and accepts gross margins of 62-64% to win volume, but it does not systematically pass on scale savings in the way of Costco or Amazon.

ns4.evidence: AI networking growth and campus expansion should make Arista larger, but NVIDIA's rise to #1 in data-centre Ethernet switching makes a clearly stronger position uncertain.

va2.evidence: It solves the painful problem of moving huge amounts of data reliably among hundreds of thousands of AI chips and servers, where network failures waste expensive GPU time.

tn1.evidence: Arista was founded in 2004 to build high-speed Ethernet for cloud-scale data centres and now sells the network infrastructure layer for AI, so it was built for this trend.

tn2.evidence: Many investors see Arista as a switch supplier to two hyperscalers, while it is becoming a broader AI, campus and SD-WAN platform with more than 10,000 customers, though this gap is widely discussed.

tn3.evidence: It is a large US company (about $249B market value), not Chinese, not a commodity producer or airline, not seasonal and not a startup.

tn4.evidence: It passes all three: revenue grew every year from 2020 to 2025, net income was $3,511.4M in 2025, and it has $13,343.3M of cash and investments with no debt.

tn5.evidence: Arista has no debt, and free cash flow was positive in Q1 2025 ($613.3M), Q2 2025 ($1,176.1M), the second half of 2025 combined, Q1 2026 ($1,639.0M) and Q2 2026 ($1,053.3M).

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 28.6% in 2025 to $9,005.7M and 36.5% in the first half of 2026.

tn7.evidence: 2025 revenue growth of 28.6% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 47.2% gives about 75.8, well above 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue grew 28.6% while operating expenses grew 23.7% to $1,912.6M, and in the first half of 2026 revenue grew 36.5% against 20.9% for operating expenses.

tn9.evidence: It avoids every instant kill: about $249B market cap, no debt, short interest about 0.9% of float, 42.8% operating margin, 28.6% revenue growth that is accelerating, no misses in the last four quarters and founded in 2004.

tn10.evidence: There is no major regulatory or legal threat to the business; co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim's 2024 SEC insider-trading settlement involved his personal trades in another company.

tn11.evidence: Arista provides high-speed switches, routers and EOS software that help cloud, AI and enterprise operators move data reliably at scale, and charges for hardware plus support and software subscriptions.

tn13.evidence: Scorecard total 110 of 130: cash vs debt 10, revenue growth 10, operating margin 10, short interest 10, institutional ownership (73.1%) 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return (about +700% vs SPY's +73%) 10, moat 5, CEO 10, recession-proof pricing power 5, secular trend 10, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew and operating margin expanded every year from 2021 to 2025 and cash always exceeded debt, but free cash flow fell from $951.1M in 2021 to $448.2M in 2022.

tn15.evidence: With no debt there is no interest to cover, assets excluding goodwill ($23,304.0M) are 2.61 times liabilities ($8,922.4M), the current ratio is 2.96 and liabilities are 0.60 times equity.

tn18.evidence: Jayshree Ullal has an excellent 18-year record as CEO (revenue from $2,317.5M in 2020 to $9,005.7M in 2025 with margins rising), but she is not a founder and sells rather than buys shares in the open market.

tn20.evidence: Arista beat consensus EPS in each of the last eight quarters, most recently $1.02 vs $0.86 in Q2 2026.

tn21.evidence: There is no sign of fraud, acquisition sprees or an auditor change (EY), and inventory rose only 12.8% in H1 2026 against 36.5% revenue growth, but gross margin is edging down and insiders keep selling while the stock rises.

tn22.evidence: It has $9,005.7M of revenue, $4,252.4M of free cash flow and no need to sell shares, so it is not a hype trap.

tn24.evidence: At $195.42, a 10% discount rate, a 44.6% FCF margin (3-year average) and 4% terminal growth imply about 35% annual revenue growth for five years, close to the 36.5% it is delivering in 2026 but above 2025's 28.6%.

tn25.evidence: With 3-year average growth of 27.3%, a 44.6% 3-year average FCF margin, 4% terminal growth, a 12% discount rate and $13,343.3M of net cash, value is about $112 per share, below $195.42.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of about 47 on FY2026 consensus EPS of $4.12 and expected EPS growth of about 38% gives a PEG of about 1.2, above 1.
